chapters.title: Chapter 3: Switching Costs and Network Effects

lessons.title: Winner Takes Most? Testing Network Effect Claims in Indian Platforms

body.text: Almost every platform company claims a network effect in its IPO document. Very few can prove it. The proof is never in user numbers. It is in pricing, costs, and margins that improve as the network grows.

children.text: The previous lesson explained how network effects work. This lesson gives you the toolkit to test whether a listed Indian platform actually has one. That matters because network effect stories command some of the highest valuations on the NSE, and the gap between the story and the evidence has cost investors a great deal.

body.title: Indian platform listings and what came next

events.title: Zomato lists
events.description: Issued at ₹76 a share. The stock rises strongly on debut, then falls to around ₹40 during 2022 as losses and competition worry investors.

events.title: Paytm, Nykaa, and Policybazaar list
events.description: Paytm (One97 Communications) is issued at ₹2,150 and falls sharply on its first day. It trades far below its IPO price for years afterwards.

events.title: Zomato turns profitable
events.description: Zomato reports its first quarterly profits, and the stock rises several-fold from its 2022 lows as unit economics visibly improve.

events.title: RBI action on Paytm Payments Bank
events.description: Regulatory restrictions on Paytm's associate bank hit its payments business, showing how fragile a platform's position can be.

events.title: Swiggy lists
events.description: The food delivery rival joins the market, confirming a listed duopoly in food delivery and quick commerce.

children.text: Investors who bought the network effect story at listing had very different outcomes depending on which platform they chose and when. The difference was not the story in each prospectus. It was whether the numbers that follow a real network effect eventually showed up.
Test 1: Can the Platform Raise Its Take Rate?

markDefs.definition: Platform revenue as a percentage of the gross value of transactions on it (GMV or GOV). A rising take rate without falling volumes signals pricing power over both sides of the network.

children.text: A platform earns a cut of the value flowing through it. That cut is its
. If the network is genuinely valuable, merchants, restaurants, or sellers will accept a slightly higher cut rather than leave, because that is where the customers are.

body.title: Calculate the Take Rate
body.prompt: A listed marketplace reports GMV of ₹7,500 crore and platform revenue of ₹1,650 crore for the year. What is its take rate?
body.explanation: Take rate = ₹1,650 crore ÷ ₹7,500 crore × 100 = 22%. Now check the trend: if last year it was 20% and GMV still grew strongly, suppliers accepted a higher cut, which is evidence the network holds real value.

body.text: GMV alone is a vanity metric. It can be inflated by discounts the platform itself funds. Always look at revenue and take rate alongside it, and read the fine print on how the company defines GMV, since definitions differ across Indian platforms.

children.text: Test 2: Do Unit Economics Improve with Scale?

markDefs.definition: Revenue from an order minus the variable costs of fulfilling it (delivery, discounts, payment charges), before fixed costs like technology and head office. Often shown per order or as a percentage of GMV.

children.text: A real network effect makes each transaction more profitable as the network gets denser. In delivery businesses, more orders in the same area mean shorter trips per order and less need for discounts. Track

body.caption: Illustrative: per-order economics of a delivery platform as density improves

children.text: Every line moves in the right direction at once: slightly higher order values, a higher take rate, cheaper delivery through density, and fewer discounts because customers no longer need to be bribed. Contribution per order grows from ₹5 to ₹39. That is what a working network looks like in the numbers.

body.title: Why contribution margin matters more than revenue growth

children.text: Fixed costs such as technology teams, offices, and brand advertising do not rise much with each extra order. Once contribution per order is positive and growing, every additional order helps cover those fixed costs, and eventually the business turns profitable at the operating level.

If contribution per order is negative, growth makes losses bigger, not smaller. A platform losing money on each order cannot grow its way to profit. It must fix unit economics first. This is the single most important question to ask of any loss-making platform.

When a network effect is working, users arrive through word of mouth and because the other side of the network is already there. Marketing spend as a percentage of revenue should fall over time. If a platform must keep spending the same or more to grow, it is buying users, not attracting them.

body.label: Proven network moats in India
body.value: Look for years of profits, not years of growth
body.context: Info Edge (Naukri) and IndiaMART built profitable, cash-generative marketplaces long before the 2021 platform wave. Their network effects show up in margins, not just user counts.

body.title: Read the Signals
body.question: A listed e-commerce platform reports 45% GMV growth. Its take rate fell from 16% to 13%, marketing spend rose from 20% to 26% of revenue, and losses widened. What do these numbers most likely indicate?
options: A strong network effect accelerating growth
Growth being bought through lower commissions and higher spending, with no proof of a network effect
A mature platform harvesting its network moat
body.explanation: A falling take rate means sellers are paying less, rising marketing means users need more incentive, and widening losses mean scale is not helping. Strong GMV growth here is the cost of buying volume, not the reward of a network effect.

body.title: Complete the Principle
body.textWithBlank: If a platform loses money on every order, growth makes its losses ___.
body.explanation: Negative contribution per order means every extra order adds to losses. Unit economics must turn positive before scale can deliver profits.

body.title: The Quick Commerce Prospectus
body.scenario: A quick commerce company files for an IPO on the NSE. It promises 10-minute delivery in 30 cities and describes a "powerful network effect between customers, dark stores, and brands". Orders have tripled in two years. It discloses that contribution margin is −3% of GMV, marketing is 12% of revenue and rising, and two larger listed rivals operate in the same cities. Brands list on all three apps.
body.prompt: Run the scorecard. Does the network effect claim hold up, and what would change your mind?
body.modelAnswer: On the scorecard, the claim is not proven. Contribution margin is negative, so growth is increasing losses. Marketing spend is rising, so users are being bought. Brands list on all three apps and customers can easily keep several apps, so multi-homing is high. Two larger rivals in the same cities mean density advantages are not clearly in its favour. Quick commerce does have some density economics: more orders per dark store lower the cost per order. But those are scale economies within each city, not a network moat that stops rivals. What would change your mind: contribution margin turning positive and rising in its oldest cities; marketing falling as a share of revenue while orders keep growing; take rates or ad income from brands rising without losing listings; and holding or gaining share in cities where it competes with larger rivals, without heavier discounts. Until then, value it as a fast-growing, loss-making retailer, not a network moat.

body.title: Score a Listed Platform
steps: Pick one listed Indian platform company and download its latest investor presentation from its website or the NSE
Find GMV or GOV and revenue for the last three years and calculate the take rate each year
Find contribution margin or contribution per order and note the trend
Calculate marketing or advertising spend as a percentage of revenue for each year
Search the concall transcript for mentions of competition, discounts, and market share
Fill in the six-row scorecard from this lesson and decide: proven, improving, or unproven

body.text: Companies and share prices mentioned are historical illustrations from public information, not investment recommendations. Unit economics and marketing figures are hypothetical. Platform metrics are defined differently across companies; read each company's definitions before comparing.

points: Network effect claims are common in platform IPOs; the proof lies in pricing, unit economics, and margins, not user counts
Test 1: a stable or rising take rate with growing volumes shows the network has pricing power
Test 2: contribution per order should rise as the network gets denser; negative unit economics make growth increase losses
Test 3: marketing spend should fall as a share of revenue if users arrive because of the network
Also check market share stability, multi-homing, and whether operating margins improve with scale
Info Edge and IndiaMART show proven network moats through years of profits, while several 2021 platform IPOs traded far below their issue prices as the evidence lagged the story
